messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elias had never considered the night the city’s patrol car boxed him in until the tactical lights cut through his studio. He was forty-two, a graphic designer accustomed to quiet hours, when the siren’s wail shattered his routine. Two officers had approached with aggressive posture, their hands hovering near their duty belts. When a fleeing suspect stumbled against Elias’s porch railing, the encounter escalated into a forceful takedown. Elias watched, paralyzed, as the suspect’s jacket tore open, revealing a deep, weeping laceration across his shoulder and a split lip that bled freely onto the concrete. Over the following weeks, the sight of similar wounds on television or on the street would instantly pull him back, forcing the memory of the takedown to resurface with full intensity. Each sudden recall brought such overwhelming emotion that Elias would have to physically stop what he was doing, his breath catching in his throat. When his wife tried to gently ask what was wrong, he would lose the thread of his story, unable to explain clearly how a routine evening had fractured into chaos. His negative appraisals began to color every subsequent experience. He was certain the system had failed to deliver justice, leaving a deep sense of injustice that festered, and he believed nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. This bitter belief warped his perception of everyday encounters, making ordinary police patrols or authority figures feel like immediate provocations rather than background noise. Whenever a patrol car rolled past or a uniformed officer came into view, that direct trigger immediately flooded his nervous system, leaving his body constantly tense and ready to react to danger. His deep sense of injustice and belief that his life was destroyed directly intensified his threat system, ensuring his body remained unable to relax even in the safety of his own bed. His conviction that his world had been destroyed made the trauma feel more immediate, which in turn made the original memories feel more vivid and inescapable. As the memories returned with greater frequency, they directly amplified his hypervigilance, flooding his nervous system before he could escape. To manage the crushing weight of these returning memories, Elias developed habits that slowly isolated him. The intrusive thoughts and sudden flashbacks drove him to spend long hours on his phone, playing games or scrolling through websites to keep his mind occupied. He avoided people, canceling dinner plans with his wife and steering clear of crowded spaces. These maladaptive strategies, initially meant to shield him, soon reinforced his fear network. By constantly distracting himself, he never allowed his brain to process the event, which meant the unprocessed memories only grew sharper and more frequent. His screen escape and mental distraction actually amplified his triggers; the silence left by his avoidance made any sudden noise or sight of authority feel like an invasion. This avoidance also fed his threat system, keeping his body on high alert and preventing him from ever relaxing. Conversely, his escalating threat state—his constant physical tension and exit-planning—made the memories feel more urgent, pulling him further into the cycle. He would catch himself scanning every room for escape routes before sitting down, his anxiety spiking whenever a police cruiser passed, only to retreat to his study and dive back into digital noise, trapping himself in a self-reinforcing loop that left him exhausted and disconnected. At forty-six, Elias sat in his darkened studio, the glow of his monitor reflecting in his tired eyes. His design deadlines piled up, but he found himself staring at blank canvases, his work suffering as his mind fixated on the unfairness of it all. What finally brought him to seek help was the morning he realized he could no longer look at his wife without fearing he would collapse under the weight of his own dread. He hoped for relief from the suffocating tension, but he feared that stepping out of his carefully constructed avoidance would leave him exposed to a world that had already taken everything from him.
